newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bavarian retailers agree to wage deal.
newsitem.headline: Bavarian retailers agree to wage deal.

text.p: Retail unions and employers in the west German state of Bavaria late on Monday reached a wage agreement, signalling the drawn out industry conflict and associated strikes may be nearing an end.

The union and employers said they had agreed on a 1.85 percent pay rise and a non-cash allowance for the planned extension of shopping hours for around 320,000 shop workers in Bavaria. The deal was backdated to May 1 and will run for 12 months.

The deal, closely mirroring an earlier agreement reached almost one month ago in the west German state of North-Rhine Westphalia, was hammered out in the eleventh round of talks and is in line with pay rises of around two percent reached in other sectors this year.

Local union representatives said they regarded the deal as a pilot agreement for three million shopworkers nationwide. Earlier the North-Rhine Westphalia deal also was seen as a pilot agreement even though many employers complained that the deal was too expensive.
It also includes a 20 percent allowance to compensate for the extension of shop opening hours from November. This will be paid in the form of free time, not in cash.
Dieter Hoebusch, an employer representative, said "we think we have helped many others facing wage conflicts with this deal."
Representatives for the unions said that the Bavarian deal shows the stalemate in the German retail wage disputes can be solved.
Rudolf Pruss, a representative for the retailers' union in the Saar region, still trying to strike a deal, said "the Bavarian deal can lend a bit of fuel to our talks."
Meanwhile strikes in the retail sector continued with both the white collar workers union DAG and the HBV banking and shopworkers' union on Tuesday calling for full day strikes in the Berlin area.
Some 400 to 500 workers walked off the job at the Karstadt und Wertheim stores on Schlossstrasse and from the Hertie store on Bundesallee, DAG representatives said.
